content.title: Is it safe to visit the Seychelles right now? What travellers need to know amid chikungunya disease outbreak
content.text: Those planning a trip to the Seychelles should be aware of a recent chikungunya outbreak. The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a level two warning for the East African country this month, meaning travellers visiting in the near future are advised to take enhanced precautions. Spread by infected mosquitoes, there has been an increase in the number of recorded cases in recent weeks.While travel is still permitted, the US's national public health agency is advising anyone with upcoming travel plans for the Seychelles to vaccinate themselves ahead of flying. It also advises pregnant women to reconsider visiting the Seychelles at this time, particularly if they are close to their due date, as the virus can be transmitted to the baby before birth.According to the CDC, chikungunya is also present in Bolivia and Suriname at the moment. If you're planning to travel to the Seychelles over the upcoming Eid al-Fitr public holiday, here's everything you need to know…Chikungunya outbreak: Can I still travel to the Seychelles?Yes, it's still safe to travel to the Seychelles, unless you are an expectant mother. Travel to the Seychelles is still permitted during the chikungunya outbreak, but travellers are advised to take extra precautions. These include a vaccination ahead of travel and preventative measures on the ground, such as mosquito repellent, long-sleeved clothing and keeping doors and windows closed.What is chikungunya disease?Chikungunya is a viral disease that is transmitted to humans by mosquitoes. The name is taken from a Swahili word meaning “to walk bent over”. Symptoms, which usually show four to eight days after the bite, include a rash, headache, high fever and severe joint pain that can persist for months to years. There is currently no treatment for chikungunya disease other than symptom management drugs.How to prevent chikungunya diseaseFor travellers with plans to visit any affected areas, there are a number of measures you can take to prevent contraction of chikungunya disease. These include:Vaccination before travel to outbreak areasWearing mosquito repellentKeeping arms and legs covered with clothingMaking sure all windows and doors in accommodation are kept shut or fitted with bug netsMaking sure all windows and doors in accommodation are kept shut or fitted with bug nets
